headline: Honolulu's 'Carnival of the Nearly Extinct Animals' Brings Endangered Species to Life Thr…
meta_description: A new staged production pairs orchestral music, puppetry, and dance to honor 13 species facing extinction, opening in Honolulu this September.
summary_short: A innovative musical production celebrates endangered species through orchestral movements, puppetry, and dance, premiering at Hawaii Theatre on September 18-19.
body:
A groundbreaking staged production called Carnival of the Nearly Extinct Animals will premiere at the historic Hawaii Theatre in Honolulu on September 18 and 19, bringing together musicians, dancers, and puppeteers to honor species facing extinction—including some that have already vanished. Composer Stephanie Ann Boyd created the orchestral work as a sister piece to the famous 1880s composition Carnival of the Animals by Camille Saint-Saëns, using 14 movements to tell the stories of 13 species: tigers, bees, butterflies, polar bears, hawksbill turtles, elephants, black rhinos, coral, blue whales, ivory-billed woodpeckers, passenger pigeons, gray wolves, American buffalo, and the kāhuli snail native to Hawaii. The production pairs the Hawaii Symphony Orchestra's score with dancers from Ballet Hawaii, handcrafted animal puppets by Obie Award-winning puppeteer Greg Corbino, and narration by Hawaiian actor Moses Goods reading poems written by local students.

Each movement translates the character of its species into sound. The tiger begins with a roar of cellos and trombones, ending with a harp playing the chuff sound tigers make. Floating violins represent bees and butterflies, while bassoons convey a hawksbill turtle gliding through water. The gray wolves and American buffalo movements celebrate recovery from near-extinction, their howling transformed into triumphant songs.

The kāhuli snail movement carries particular poignancy for Hawaii. Once so abundant that their shells reportedly created an eerie, magical sound throughout the forests, these native snails have been devastated: Hawaii once held roughly 750 species of land snails, but state biologists estimate up to 90 percent of that diversity is now gone. Every surviving kāhuli in the genus Achatinella is federally listed as endangered. Cellos carry their song now, floating over harp and string harmonics—a musical memorial to what the islands have lost.
quick_facts: Opens at Hawaii Theatre in Honolulu, September 18-19
Honors 13 endangered or extinct species through orchestral music
Features puppets handcrafted by Obie Award-winning artist Greg Corbino
Hawaii lost up to 90% of its 750 native land snail species
Inspired by Saint-Saëns' 1880s 'Carnival of the Animals' composition
